newsitem.title: USA: U.S. government seeks to raise foreign spending.
newsitem.headline: U.S. government seeks to raise foreign spending.

text.p: The Clinton administration, saying future events in the former Soviet Union posed the most serious threat to the United States, on Thursday proposed raising foreign spending to reassert U.S. world leadership.
The White House called for a seven percent rise in its international affairs budget to nearly $19.5 billion, following years of declines.
Most of this was accounted for by a $1.1 billion rise in foreign aid, including a 44 percent hike -- to $900 million -- in aid to former Soviet states.
The proposal was part of a $1.69 trillion federal budget for 1998 submitted to Congress by President Bill Clinton.
Although foreign affairs accounts for little more than one percent of the budget, few issues raise more hackles in the Republican-controlled legislature.
But the foreign spending proposal received a cautious welcome from New York Republican Benjamin Gilman, chairman of the House of Representatives International Relations Committee.

Gilman said that while he did not endorse everything in it, "with our new secretaries of state and defence, I think we can forge a bipartisan consensus with the administration on the basis of this budget request."

The proposal said a less orderly world created new challenges to U.S. security, and this was no time to fall back into "isolationism and protectionism" by failing to fund Washington's mission of global leadership.

It said that "perhaps the most serious national security threat facing the nation today hinges on the course of events over the next few years in the New Independent States of the former Soviet Union".

The large vote for opponents of Boris Yeltsin in Russia's 1996 presidential election, due to the country's "severe economic distress", was a warning, it said. It was "absolutely critical" to back democratic reform and free markets in the region.
The proposed allocation to support the Middle East peace process -- most of it military and civil aid to Israel and Egypt -- was increased slightly over 1997 to $5.3 billion.
More than half the $100 million increase was accounted for by an initial U.S. contribution to a planned Middle East development bank.

The request contained details of an already publicised plan to help pay off arrears of more than $1 billion in U.N. dues by seeking a one-off advance appropriation of $921 million to become available in 1999.
The money would only be paid over if Washington and the United Nations agreed on cuts in Washington's annual dues -- a key demand of the world body's many foes in Congress.
But the request warned that U.S. leadership in the international system was threatened by Washington's failure to pay its bills.
"America's failure to meet its obligations has undercut our efforts to achieve reforms on which the administration and Congress agree," it said.

The budget also proposed an eight percent rise -- to $230 million -- in funding for the State Department's narcotics and anti-crime programmes. Most of the increase would go to programmes in Peru, it said.
